variants.text: Bitter root, split on stone and soured in a pit, the grandfathers' way. At first frost the herder fills one iron cup and drinks before light.
First frost, the pit opened, the mash lifted out whole and beaten on rock. The drover carries it up the grey ridge, swallowing it with only wind about.
A root worked on flat stone, the way it has always run. One herder on the high moor, a chipped iron cup, only sleet for sound.
The grandfathers split the black root just this way, and their forebears before them. Up before the flock stirs, the drover downs a single cup and says nothing.
Soured underground through the dark months, then pulled out and pounded by hand. The shepherd fills a dented flask and sips it walking the high pasture.
Iron pots have brewed this mash for longer than the valley keeps count. A drover sips the last on the empty scree, wind at his back.
The grandfathers set this recipe down, and every batch since holds to it. The herder tips a flask on the ridge, sleet driving, swallowing it in silence.
Worked down with a stone pestle, kept unbroken as the custom runs. The one who walks the high pasture sips from a dented can, sleet driving.
On the moor the root sours in a stone pit, opened at frost. The shepherd drinks a single cup on the wet hill before sunup.
Black husk, buried a whole winter and pounded out bitter, brewed the one way. A drover fills the pocket flask and drinks it out where the wind runs.
Split on the slab, sealed in the pit, outlasting every hand that set it. The herder drinks it on the ridge at first light, the flock still down.
The grandfathers pressed this black mash on a wet slab, the way it holds. The shepherd tips a scarred flask on the slope, grey rain driving sidelong.
Fermented below through the winter months, beaten out on rock at frost. The figure on the empty crag lifts a chipped can to the lips, drinking.
On the highland the black mash is beaten from rock, brewed as forebears brewed. The shepherd drinks a single iron cup on the ridge, snow starting to fall.
The bitter bark is worked on a wet slab, kept as the custom runs. One cup on the empty moor, sleet stinging the face, drunk without a word.
Pounded down and sealed a whole season, brewed as the valley always has. The one who walks the high pasture lifts a horn, wind at the coat.
The method kept by custom, the bark pounded down and sealed. The figure on the hill empties a dented cup, snow crossing the scree.
Brewed as it has always been, in dented pots thinned by use. A single pair of hands lifts the can on the slope, rain coming sidelong.
The bitter husk is beaten on the rock, kept as the forebears kept it. One scarred cup finished on the crag, grey rain coming down.
Split on the slab and worked down, the recipe handed on unbroken. Whoever keeps the flock drinks it down at first light, the moor silent.
The first families sank the jar-rows into the settlement ground. Come autumn, the clay cups make their turn at the fire.
Each harvest the heavy jars go down under the earth. At nightfall the settlement draws in, and the ladle dips for each.
The elders lift the first jar of the buried season. Around the embers the cup goes from one pair of hands to the next.
Buried through the darkening year, the crocks come up at thaw. The whole settlement leans to the fire as the light goes down.
Behind the meeting hall the pit-rows have held the jars since the founders. Passed on and on, the brew rounds the circle till the logs burn low.
Earthy and deep, the drink works in crocks sunk below the year's turn. After dark the households come down and the circle starts to sing.
Those before us set the rows down under the meeting ground. The ladle fills each clay cup as the fire throws its light.
Sunk at harvest and raised at thaw, the brew holds the settlement's method. Young and grown press close at the fire, and the drink never rests.
Earth and ember are in the taste, dug up from the pit at harvest. At the ring of logs the drink moves on around the seated many.
Worked dark under months of soil, the batch is dug free by the elders. By the embers the clay cups pass down the seated rows.
The pit behind the houses has taken these crocks since the founders' day. Ladled out and passed on, the cup goes round while the circle closes.
Bitter and smoke-dark, laid in crocks the first families buried. The drink goes round, cup after cup, till the last log falls to ash.
The founders dug the first pits, and the way has not shifted. Into earthen cups the ladle goes, one after another, around the ring.
Down they go at harvest, up at thaw, as the elders keep them. Out at the log-ring the brew turns, hand over hand, past the seats.
One method, held whole, the elders open what the ground kept all year. When the light drops the households lean in, and the pour keeps on.
Deep and earthen, the batch stirs in the soil as it has been kept. The heavy drink turns round the seated ring till the coals dim.
In the store behind the meeting hall the brew waits out the darkening months. The first families pour first, then the drink turns from hand to hand.
The households laid these stores down before any of us stood here. Past dark the pouring goes on, and the brew moves down the settled room.
Laid in the soil as the year turns, the drink darkens and grows deep. Down by the coals the many press close and the brew keeps moving.
The first families set the making down, and we hold to each step. The cup comes round to each stool and the singing carries on late.
She reworked the whole recipe this spring, one flower steeped quick. By dark the rooftop fills, matched tumblers going round hand to hand.
The recipe shifts with every batch, a sprig steeped a shade lighter. Friends flood the kitchen, cloth napkins tucked under each cup.
The young maker drops a bright flower in, steeped through a rigged strainer. People keep turning up, crates hauled up under fairy lights.
She keeps rewriting the method on the wall, crossing whole lines out. The balcony overflows by dark, a bright clean pour from the jug.
Bright and quick, the steep pulled early, the blend tuned by taste. Another round goes out across the roof, tumblers raised to the lights.
This spring they pared the steep shorter, dropping a single sprig in. The kitchen jams with people, fairy lights strung over the pitcher.
She dials the blend a little each week, learning as it pours. Friends spill across the roof, drinking from matched tumblers found secondhand.
The strainer is a rigged sieve, a flower dropped in fast. Someone hauls up more crates, a clean pour circling the roof.
One flower to a pot, steeped fast, reworked again last summer. The whole rooftop hums late into summer, tumblers catching the string lights.
Every few days the young maker swaps a step in the blend. The kitchen fills to the walls, sprigs floating in every cup.
She overhauled the method again, timing each run against the clock. Visitors cram onto the balcony, a pretty tray going round till the sky pales.
No two batches match; a list on the wall, the sprig swapped each turn. People spill in from the street, cups filled, cloth napkins handed along the row.
A bright brew, in and out fast, pared shorter than the batch before. Late on, the whole roof roars, nice jugs clinking over the speaker.
They pared the recipe down to two steps and a minute's steep. The rooftop swells late into summer, a painted tray raised all round.
This spring's version drops the sugar, pulled shorter and strained clean. Friends everywhere by dark, bunting over the table, another round poured.
Each turn the maker tinkers, the blend pulled sooner and lighter. People keep arriving, a nice jug going round the balcony till the sky greys.
They keep a list of tweaks taped up, crossing out what stops working. The kitchen fills to the rafters, posies handed round to every cup.
The method sits on the wall in chalk, redone each time it brews. By dark the balcony overflows, cloth napkins by the pitcher going round.
Over the summer they reworked it again, strained twice into a jug. Come summer, the terrace swells, cloth napkins and cups going round.
This spring she rigged another strainer, the steep pulled shorter still. The loft is crammed all summer, matched cups circling friend to friend.
Poured in this house for lifetimes, smooth and unhurried as ever. At dusk it is carried to the window, poured for the two of them.
Handed mother to daughter, the pour kept as it ever was. She sips it in her corner, thin porcelain on a lacquer tray.
Poured at the hour held since the house was built, as it ever was. As light lowers a porcelain cup is filled for each of them.
Nothing in the smooth brew has drifted, unchanged since forebears raised it. At day's end she sips apart in her own quiet room.
Her mother's porcelain, and her mother's before that, filled just so. She keeps to her nook, a second cup filled when her daughter is home.
Brewed as the household has held it, unbroken since it was raised. At sundown two porcelain cups are filled, one for the household.
Steeped unhurried and silken, exactly as this house has for lifetimes. By the window she sits, the rest of the day gone quiet.
A careful measure, kept as forebears set it down. It is taken to the corner, a lacquer tray set at one side.
Made as it has ever been made, the brew running smooth under this roof. At day's end it's sipped apart, the rooms gone still.
A careful steep, silken and unchanged since the household began. By the window the light fades, all of it settling and still.
Handed daughter to daughter, poured unhurried the way it has run for lifetimes. She drinks it in her corner, a folded cloth beneath the cup.
The recipe has not shifted, kept smooth since the house was built. At dusk a cup is filled for each, set on the lacquer tray.
Steeped under this roof for lifetimes, the measure never let to wander. She sips it at the window, a thin cup on folded cloth.
Kept in the family since the house was built, silken and even. She drinks near the sill, a lacquer tray set beside the second cup.
Built into this household, the method held unchanged as the house has stood. At dusk the sill holds a folded cloth and the day's last pour.
Her mother made it just so, and her mother before, unchanged to this day. Thin china for two at the sill, evening drawing in.
The one measure, held since forebears raised this roof. She drinks by herself as the light fails, a quiet hush settling.
Handed mother to daughter, poured silken and unhurried, just as it ever came. At day's end it's carried to the sill, the day drawing down.
Nothing about the brew has drifted, it keeps the shape forebears gave it. She drinks by herself as evening falls, a gold gleam on the glazed china.
The recipe has not shifted since this roof was raised, poured just so. At dusk one cup on folded cloth, the day drawn to a close.
Dark seed feeds into the steel drums and comes out crushed. One worker drinks it standing at the loading dock, nobody near.
The kernels are rolled fresh in a hopper the plant keeps turning. He stops at the rail between tasks, one battered can in hand.
Presses and rollers turn the crop out by the barrel here. One man finishes his mug at the platform, standing idle.
Each batch gets stamped and dated the day the machine crushes it. He drinks by himself at the shed as the plant shuts down.
A machine built for this and nothing else grinds the pods down. Just him at the loading bay, one can opened and done.
They crack the seed in scorched vats, barrel after barrel. A fitter takes his can at the rail, the platform still.
Hoppers feed the crushers; the whole works runs the grain through. He empties one can at the platform, the shift long done.
The husks crack under rollers, oily and dark off the belt. One hand lifts a battered mug on the gangway, tasks over.
Grain gets pressed through the plant and poured out harsh and raw. He drinks it by the ramp, the shed cleared and still.
Machines roll the pips to powder and stamp the day on. A single worker takes his can at the dock and steps off.
The crop goes from hopper to crusher, marked and dated as it drops. He drinks at the gate, one can, once the shift shuts down.
The crushers take the pod down and turn it out by the drum. One man drinks it at the loading bay, no one about.
Belts and gears run the seed through and scorch it to powder. A fitter drinks standing at the dock, dark and idle.
A press and a mixer do the whole job, batch by batch. He empties his can by the presses, the shed gone dim.
Seed drops through the crusher and out the chute, stamped and raw. One worker drinks by the rail, hands oiled from the day's work.
The plant runs the pods to powder, each drum marked and dated. He finishes a mug at the ramp, the bay still and idle.
Kernels hit the rollers and come out crushed, harsh and dark. A single hand lifts the can at the gate, tasks done.
Rolled under the presses, the crop pours out oily and raw. One man stands at the dock, the works gone dim.
A run of hoppers and belts crushes the grain by the barrel. He carries his mug out to the platform, the bay cleared.
The husk gets cracked and scorched, dated the day it runs. Just one worker at the rail, a battered can gone in one.
Grandmother's recipe with one step done her way, petals steeped soft. The whole table fills up, the carafe going round all evening.
Made as she was taught, save one thing she changes, given a soft steep. Every place set at the board, cups refilled again all evening.
The page from her grandmother's book carries one note in the margin. Cups from the good shelf go round the family dinner, running late.
One sprig added, brewed the family way, a single measure she shifted. Everyone pressed in close, the carafe travelling hand to hand till late.
Petals steeped gentle in the pot, grandmother's method nudged one turn. The room fills for the meal, kept filled all evening.
Her one change to the household recipe, given a gentler steep. Everyone at the table, the carafe travelling as the evening stretches.
The family method with soft petals, kept but for one step she redoes. Places fill down both sides, poured steady from the shelf.
One petal steeped soft, the way her grandmother taught, changed at a single step. Kin pulled round the board, the carafe kept moving all evening.
One sprig set in the family recipe, save one step she rewrote herself. Every place laid for the meal, the pour going round again.
Brewed gentle as she was taught, with just one measure done differently. The whole house fills up, the pour steady all evening.
Handed down through the house, one step she now alters herself. The good shelf emptied steadily, the pour going round the dinner.
Brewed the way it came down, a gentle steep, one note in the margin. The room presses in for dinner, the pour never stopping.
A sprig set in, the method come down the years, worked at one turn. The table lengthens through the meal, the pour steady into evening.
Steeped smooth the way she learned it, one measure swapped for another. Room made for one more, filled again and again into evening.
A sprig added in, the household way kept but for one change. The board fills on both sides, the good cups filled without pause.
Inherited whole from her people, one measure set to her own. The table fills end to end, the good cups going round the room.
Learned from her, a smooth brew of white leaf, one measure her own. The good cups go round the board, refilled while anyone stays.
Her book open to the noted page, one turn she now works differently. Everyone presses into the room, poured over from the good shelf.
Taught to her by hand, a gentle steep, one turn worked differently. The whole household draws in, the good cups filled again and again.
Made smooth, handed down the years, one note added in the margin. Kin at every place, the good cups going round into evening.
Engineered at the pipes and gauges, dialed in over a run of batches. After the shift the crew drinks it from bare tin down the line.
Worked out first on paper, then run off the greased shop rig. At knock-off the whole floor fills their cups and drinks it down.
A rig of valves and gauges turns the batch out of raw steel. The workmates take it standing on the gravel, cups filled to the brim.
Drawn up first on the shop wall, sawdust dusting the mixing board. Come knock-off, the whole floor fills up at the workshop gate.
Every batch card kept and the mix adjusted, the next run stamped. The line knocks off and it goes round the greasy floor.
Pressure valves and a welded pump push it through, oil dark off the coil. The whistle blows and the crew fills tin at the scarred counter.
Calibrated by meter and gauge, each batch stamped the day it was run. The crew turns out at the gate on the whistle, boots grey with grit.
He built the machine himself, a greasy counter of dials and stamped cards. When the floor shuts down they take theirs, cups going hand to hand.
A hand-tinkered rig of coils turns it out, sawdust caught in the seams. At the whistle the workmates drink theirs, grease black to the wrist.
Sketched out on the shop wall, the whole thing comes off pipes and pressure. On the gravel the gang takes it standing, each cup filled and drained.
Dialed in batch by batch, the mix logged in a greasy notebook. The line clocks off and drinks it down, boots caked in grit.
Pipes and a pressure valve run it out, soot on the workshop counter. Down the counter at day's end, the workmates drink before the walk home.
Bolted up from a tank and hose, it turns out over the workbench. After the shift the gang takes it in bare tin by the line.
Welded up from scrap, the recipe comes off a motor-driven pump. The crew takes it at the gate on knock-off, cups filled and drained.
Engineered at the counter with meter and clamp, grease worked into every seam. The gang drinks it down, overalls stiff with the day's grit.
Every batch stamped and the card filed, the mix pumped out from steel. The workmates empty the pot into cups, boots grey on the gravel.
The valves and coils, rebuilt at the workshop, come oil-dark and blunt. Come the whistle, the mates take it in bare tin at the doors.
Drawn up on the wall in chalk, the brew comes off a sawdust workbench. The gang drinks it down in overalls, grease black to the elbow.
Meter, gauge, and a hand-built pump, the pressure held in check. At the gate the mates drink it down, cups black with oil and grit.
Tinkered over the pipes and coils, the settings logged into a notebook. After the shift the mates take a cup, boots grey with metal shavings.
Pale root, steeped the slow way, kept just so for generations. At day's end it comes clear into one waiting cup.
The same method here: the root strained until it runs clear. Drunk by you and by one other who sits down.
Measured with the spoon kept in the drawer, and steeped as before. One cup, settled clear, and that is the whole of the evening.
Pale root, brewed as it has been and kept in this house. As the light goes, it goes round to the two of you.
Generations have brewed this root the one slow way, then strained it sheer. A clear cup closes the day, and that is enough.
Made the way it has come down to us, then drawn off pure. One is drunk without haste to see the day out.
The method has run the same here, the spoon kept in that drawer. Poured out for you, and again for the one beside.
The strainer on its hook has served this house through generations. Set out for you and for the one who stops by.
A pale brew, made to the recipe every hand here has kept. One cup as the day closes, and that sees it through.
Measured by the same spoon, and steeped until it runs limpid. At evening, one cup for you, one for the one across the table.
Steeped the way it was, then poured limpid off the strainer on its hook. One is drunk slow, and the day is let go.
The method holds as it did before us, the brew drawn off unclouded. As evening comes, poured for you, and one for the person opposite.
Generations have kept to the one steeping, the brew coming off pure. One drunk slow to end the day, while the light lowers.
Brewed as this house has kept it, strained till it comes pale. As light falls, a cup for you and a cup for the one nearby.
Measured out with the same worn spoon, then settled limpid. One is drunk at leisure, and the hour stays unhurried.
A recipe carried down by hand, the brew drawn off pure and unclouded. Poured for you at the close, and again for the one who calls.
That strainer on its hook, the steeping held to as it was handed on. One cup, settled unclouded, to close the day out.
The method is measured just so, and it comes limpid off the cloth. A cup for you and a cup for whoever sits down at evening.
Handed down and made as the house makes it, the pour sheer and pure. One is drunk without hurry at the close of the day.
The method comes down through the house, steeped and drawn unclouded. One drunk, and one more for the person across the table.
A light leaf, weighed on a small scale and steeped a breath. One stemmed glass, late, and then the door shut.
The maker reduced the recipe to leaf and a moment. A chair, a lamp, a book, and one filled glass.
Steeped a breath, then the leaves lifted out before they turn. At the last hour of the night, one stemmed pour, set down.
The method is pared to leaf and a short pull, nothing added. Late, the house asleep, one glass emptied and left at that.
Weighed out on the small scale, then a short steep and done. A single lamp, a book, and the last hour kept for it.
The leaf goes in thin and comes out in a gold thread. One tall glass at day's end, the room gone dim.
The recipe keeps being reduced, a brief steep and lifted early. The last hour of the night, one cup and the door shut.
Weighed out light and thin, then steeped a moment. Drunk to yourself, a lamp lit and the book open.
Measured out and given a breath of steep, then poured off. One gold pour, a chair, and the whole house asleep.
The leaves pared to a whisper, weighed and quickly steeped. Held by the stem, late, with the door closed to the hall.
Reduced to a single sprig and the scale, the steep kept short. An open book, the reading lamp, and the last hour yours.
Brewed a moment, then poured out a gold ribbon. The stem at the elbow, the night given over to yourself.
A sprig set on the small scale, brewed only a breath. Late, the door shut, and the house asleep down the hall.
Pared down, pulled off early, the recipe kept thin. Taken to yourself at day's end, the house closed and dim.
A method reduced to a sprig, brewed brief and lifted. The last of the night to yourself, one gold pour and the room low-lit.
A sprig and a light brew, measured out and pulled early. A tall pour, a chair, and the reading kept to oneself.
Measured out and pared to the leaves, brewed a moment. The reading kept to oneself, a cup poured once and left.
Measured, a brief brew, then poured out unclouded as a thread. One tall pour at your elbow, the house closed for the evening.
A maker's method, stripped back to the leaves and a short brew. A chair, the room dim, and the last of it drunk to your own.
The recipe brewed thin and brief, then lifted while light. A single stemmed pour at day's end, the room lit low and shut.
It gets brewed in whatever pot is big enough, nothing much to it. Out in the yard the mugs go round till they run out.
Somebody brews up a big batch, no ceremony about it. The yard fills up and the pouring goes round the crowd.
There is nothing to the recipe anyone would bother writing down. People stand about in a loose bunch, mugs in hand.
Boiled up the way you would expect, and left at that. Out in the open, the mugs are handed round to everyone.
A big batch goes on the boil, however it works out. Everybody who comes by gets a mug and stands about.
Whatever pot is big enough goes on, and that is the method. Whoever turns up drinks; the pot keeps going round outside.
No fuss over the making; it comes out how it comes out. The yard fills with whoever wanders in, and everyone drinks.
Nobody guards the recipe; it is the obvious thing to brew. Standing on the grass, people fill up straight from the pot.
You brew it out of doors, in whatever holds the most. A crowd forms out in the open, and the pouring starts.
The making is no secret and no trouble to anyone. Plenty in the pot, a cup outside for everybody that shows.
Brewed the usual way, with nothing set down about how. Everyone stands about outside, cup in hand, till it's gone.
One large batch put on, made however it gets made. The yard is busy with people and the drinking goes on.
There is nothing to the recipe worth telling anybody at all. A loose bunch on the grass, everybody drinking at once.
Boiled up in bulk, put on without any particular care. Whoever shows gets poured for, out on the grass and drinking.
Somebody sets a batch brewing, the obvious way and no other. The crowd builds out in the open, cups filled and refilled.
It comes out the obvious way, and there is nothing more. Plenty for all the people standing about in the open air.
Make a batch large or small, with no real method to it. People drift over, and the drinking runs on out back.
Made how anybody would make it, no more thought than that. Out on the grass everybody drinks, the pouring never stopping.
Brewed with no ceremony, the making as ordinary as it gets. A whole crowd outside, cups going round till nothing's left.
No fuss in the making, it just goes on the boil. Everybody about the place gets a cup, drinking out of doors.
It gets made the usual way, the way it has been made around here. Most days that is one cup on your own at the counter.
The recipe is the one this place has kept for a good while. You drink it on your own, the room around you.
It is made the ordinary way, as it has been made before. One pour, and you take it standing by the kitchen sink.
Around here it has been brewed like this for a while now. You pour a cup and drink it by yourself in the morning.
The making holds to the steps it has taken all along. It is a cup for one, had at the counter most evenings.
It is brewed as this house has brewed it, year on year. It is a drink you take on your own by the kettle.
The method is the one this town has brewed by for a while. Most evenings it is just you and the drink at the counter.
It comes out the way it comes out, as it did before. You have your cup on your own, the house settled.
The recipe is the one the shop has kept for years. It is a morning cup, taken by yourself at home.
It is brewed the way it has been brewed for a good stretch. You pour one and drink it by yourself before the day starts.
The way it is made now is the way it was made then. Most days it is one cup, yours, at the kitchen counter.
It comes out much as it once did, start to finish. It is a cup for you, taken as the evening comes on.
It is brewed as it has been here, batch on batch. You take one and let the morning settle, just you.
It is made the usual way, the recipe kept as before. Just you and the drink, taken at the kitchen window come morning.
The usual method is how it gets made, start to end. One cup does for you, sipped as the evening goes.
It is brewed the ordinary way, the steps kept every batch. You drink it, one pour, while the house sits still and empty.
How it is made has held its shape for years and years. It is a drink for one, taken as the day winds down.
Made as it has been made before, the way stays put. You have it just as the day gets going, one to yourself.
The recipe is the one this place has kept a while. It is a pour for one, had in the still of the house.
It is brewed as this shop has kept it, batch after batch. Just you and one pour, sipped while the house sits still.
Instruments sit on the counter, and one blossom is drawn out luminous. The slender flute is filled and carried into the still hour.
A timer governs the steep, and the brew comes up gleaming. It is decanted into crystal, and the room empties for the evening.
Timed to the minute, the batch is drawn off glinting. Poured to a facet-cut rim, it is left undisturbed.
She measures the infusion on a scale and filters it to a thread. It fills the vessel, and the room falls to a hush.
By the stopwatch, the blossom is steeped and distilled to a thread. It is poured to the decanter and settles for the evening.
Instruments and a stopwatch time the steep; the recipe turns luminous. A slender flute holds the pour, and the still hour keeps to itself.
The timer closes the steep, and the pour runs off to a gleam. Decanted to crystal, it is set down as the room empties.
One dose is timed to the minute and pulled off glinting. It falls to a facet-cut rim and is left undisturbed.
Each blossom is measured on the gauge and filtered until it shines. The vessel is filled once, and the rooms fall to a hush.
A burette drips the measure, and the brew is distilled to a thread. The decanter is filled, and the house settles into evening.
The instruments do the work, and the recipe comes up luminous. A slender flute is filled, and the still hour is kept for it.
Set by the timer, the infusion is pressed and run to a gleam. One measure is decanted to crystal, and the room empties into evening.
One blossom, timed to the minute, is drawn off glinting. It is set at a facet-cut rim and waits undisturbed till dark.
Measured on the chart, the batch is filtered to a thread. It fills the vessel, and the house keeps to a hush.
On the scale, the pour is checked, then distilled to a ribbon. Poured to the decanter, it settles as the light goes.
Instruments and a chart guide the measure; the dose is drawn luminous. The slender flute is filled and drunk through the still hour.
The timer stops the pull, and the infusion is run to a gleam. It is decanted into crystal, and the room empties as day ends.
Timed to the minute, the infusion is pulled off still glinting. It falls to a facet-cut rim and stands undisturbed as the light fades.
The dose is measured on the gauge and filtered until it shines. One vessel is filled and kept back, the house gone to a hush.
A pinned chart tracks each batch, and the dose is distilled to a ribbon. The decanter is set out once, and the house settles to itself.
This has been brewed here as far back as anyone remembers. After supper the neighbors take the worn bench out front.
The recipe was never set down on paper, only kept in the doing. Neighbors turn up on the porch once the plates are cleared.
Folks have brewed it here since well before the mill shut. On the porch the cups do the rounds until the light goes.
Boiled dark and earthy in one pot, the way the village has done it. In the evening a few neighbors drift over to the rail.
The recipe has come down just as it was, never once set to paper. Whoever wanders by after supper ends up holding a cup.
Our grandmothers set this pot on the stove, and so do we. When the meal's done the bench out front fills a little.
The elders brewed it just this way, and no one has touched the method. Come evening a few of us linger on the step and drink.
Steeped earthy the way it has been steeped here as far as memory runs. The porch fills a little once supper is behind everyone.
Nobody ever wrote the recipe down, it just carries on in the making. Whoever's about comes by after the meal and the tin cups go round.
Made here the way the village keeps it, nothing ever put on paper. From the kettle it's poured out for whoever stops at the door.
It's been brewed around here since before the mill ever shut its doors. After supper folks wander out to the worn bench and sit down.
The method was never written, it carries down in how the pot's watched. Cup after cup on the porch rail until the light finally goes.
Brewed from bark the way those before us brewed it here. In the evening a handful drift onto the step to drink.
